transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Thanks. Um, well, I guess I'm here because things have just been getting really overwhelming lately, and I didn't know what else to do. I work as an animal caretaker—I've got my bachelor's in biology, actually—and the job is great, but it's super physically demanding. I'm on my feet all day with the animals, so by the time I get home, I'm just completely drained, you know? And I live by myself, so the evenings are pretty quiet. 

But lately... well, once I start eating alone at night, it just spirals. It feels like something else entirely just takes over. I just can't stop. It's the weirdest, most frustrating thing because I'm completely aware of what's happening. I'm literally standing there in my kitchen, telling myself over and over to just put the food away, like, I'm screaming in my own head to just close the cabinet, just walk into the other room, but I can't do it. My hands just keep going, and I just keep eating, even though my brain is begging me to stop. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body, and I just don't have any control anymore once I'm by myself in the evening. It's exhausting, honestly, to fight with yourself like that and lose every single time.
How do you feel after one of these episodes of eating alone at night?

How do I feel? Um, honestly, it's just this massive wave of panic. And guilt, just so much guilt. Like, the minute I finally stop eating, the reality of what I just did hits me like a ton of bricks. My stomach is physically hurting because it's so stretched out, and I'm just standing there looking at the empty wrappers and the dirty plates, and my heart starts racing. 

And because I know how digestion works—you know, with my biology background and everything—my brain immediately goes into overdrive about absorption. I just start thinking, I have to get this out. I have to undo this right now. So... I almost always end up rushing to the bathroom. I lock the door, even though I live completely alone, which is stupid, I know, but I do it anyway. And I just... I make myself throw up. 

It's just, it feels like the absolute only way to fix what I just broke. If I don't do it, the panic just keeps building and building until I feel like I'm going to jump out of my skin. I just have to get it out before the calories have a chance to settle in and actually absorb into my body. And then after I do that, after I throw up, there's this weird, brief moment of relief, like I hit a reset button. But then the shame comes right back, and I'm just sitting on the bathroom tiles, rinsing my mouth out, looking in the mirror and wondering how I let it happen again. It's just this whole exhausting cycle, and I hate it, I really do, but in that moment right after I eat, the urge to just purge it all is so overwhelming I can't even think straight until it's done.
How often do these episodes of eating alone at night and then purging happen?

Well, um, if I really think about it, looking back over the last... I'd say at least the last four months, it's been happening pretty consistently. It's usually at least one night every single week. Sometimes it feels like more, depending on how stressed I am at work or if I've had a particularly rough day with the animals. You know, like if one of the enclosures needed a deep clean or if we had a sick animal that needed extra monitoring, I come home just completely wiped out, and those are the nights it's most likely to happen. 

But yeah, for the past four months, it's been at least once a week where I just... I eat way, way more than I ever intended to. Like, I'll go into the kitchen thinking I'm just going to have a normal dinner, maybe a piece of chicken and some rice, and then before I know it, I've eaten that, and then half a loaf of bread, and a whole box of cereal, and whatever else I can get my hands on. It's just this massive amount of food, and then, like I said, the panic sets in, and I end up in the bathroom making myself throw it all up. 

It's become this terrible, predictable routine. Every week, at least once a week, for four months now. I keep telling myself at the start of every week, "Okay, this week is going to be different. I'm going to meal prep, I'm going to stick to a schedule, I'm not going to let myself get too hungry," but then Thursday or Friday rolls around, I'm exhausted, I'm alone in the apartment, and the whole cycle just repeats itself. I eat everything in sight, and then I purge. It's just... it's exhausting to even keep track of it, honestly.
Do you consider yourself underweight?

Underweight? Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I'm definitely not underweight. If anything, I'm probably right in the middle, maybe even a little heavier than I'd like to be, honestly. It's funny you ask that because, with my biology background, I actually pay a lot of attention to BMI and weight distribution and all that stuff, probably more than I should. And with my job, you know, being an animal caretaker, I have to be pretty strong. I'm hauling 50-pound bags of feed, moving heavy crates, wrestling with large dogs or trying to hold down a thrashing sheep for a vet exam. So I have a decent amount of muscle mass just from the day-to-day physical labor of it all. 

But my weight... it fluctuates a bit, but it never drops down into what anyone would call underweight. It's actually one of the things that makes me feel so crazy about this whole cycle. Like, I'm eating thousands of calories in a single sitting, and then I'm throwing it all up, but my body just kind of stays the same. Or at least, it doesn't change enough for anyone else to notice. Sometimes I look in the mirror and I feel like I look huge, like all that food I binged on somehow permanently attached itself to me even though I purged. And other times I feel like I look totally normal, which almost makes it harder because it feels like I'm hiding this massive, ugly secret in plain sight. People see me at work, and they just see a regular, healthy-looking guy who can lift a bale of hay without breaking a sweat, but they have no idea what my body goes through behind closed doors. So, yeah, no, definitely not underweight. I'm just... I'm just regular, I guess. Which is its own kind of frustrating, if that makes any sense.
Do you ever exercise excessively to try to burn off the calories from these binge eating episodes?

Exercise excessively? Um, no, not really. I mean, honestly, by the time I get home from the sanctuary, the thought of going for a run or hitting the gym is just... it's completely laughable. Like I was saying before, my job is already so intensely physical. I spend eight, sometimes ten or twelve hours a day on my feet, moving non-stop. I'm lugging around those huge 50-pound bags of specialized feed, I'm scrubbing down the large enclosures, I'm literally wrestling with livestock sometimes. 

Just the other day, actually, we had a goat that absolutely refused to let us trim its hooves, and it took three of us to safely hold him steady without stressing him out too much, and my arms were just burning by the end of it. So by the time I actually walk through my front door at night, my muscles are already aching, my back is sore, and I'm just completely, utterly drained. The physical labor is basically my workout, and it's a pretty intense one. 

So when these... these eating episodes happen, which is usually late at night when I'm already running on empty, I don't try to sweat it out. I don't hop on a treadmill or do jumping jacks or anything like that. The panic hits, and my immediate reaction is just to get it out the absolute fastest way possible, which is... well, throwing up in the bathroom, like I mentioned. I don't even think I'd have the physical energy to exercise it off even if I wanted to, because the binge itself kind of makes me feel so heavy and sluggish, and my body is already so battered from working with the animals all day. So, no, I don't do the whole excessive exercise thing. The purging is... it's the only thing I do to try and fix it.
Do you ever use laxatives or diuretics after one of these binge eating episodes?

Laxatives? Or diuretics? Um, no. No, I've never really gone down that route. Honestly, with my biology background, I just... I think too much about the human digestive tract and how long things actually take to process. Like, if you take a laxative, the food has already been sitting in your stomach, it's already moving through the small intestine, so the nutrients and, well, the massive amount of calories are already being absorbed into your bloodstream. So in my head, it just doesn't make any logical sense to use them if the whole goal is to get rid of what I just binged on. 

Plus, practically speaking, with my job at the sanctuary, I absolutely cannot afford to have, you know, unpredictable stomach issues or dehydration the next day. Imagine trying to clean out a massive, muddy enclosure or trying to wrangle a terrified, fifty-pound rescue dog while worrying about needing to sprint to the restroom because you took a laxative the night before. Or being dizzy from diuretics while carrying heavy feed bags. It would be a complete disaster, and it wouldn't be fair to the animals either. They need me present and focused. 

So, no, I stay away from those completely. For me, it's just... well, like I was saying before, after I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up because it feels like the only way to undo it before the calories settle in. It's all about the immediacy of it, you know? The panic hits the absolute second I swallow that last bite of whatever I'm eating, and I just have this overwhelming, suffocating sensation that I need to hit the reset button right that very second. If I wait, if I just let all that food sit there in my stomach, I can almost physically feel my body starting to break it down, and that thought just completely terrifies me. So throwing up is... it's immediate. It's really the only thing that gives me that instant, albeit temporary, relief. It gives me that false sense that I've somehow erased the whole mistake before it becomes a permanent part of me, without having to wait hours for a pill to kick in.
Do these episodes of binge eating and purging happen every week without fail?

Every week? Yeah. Yeah, without fail, for... gosh, at least the last four months, I'd say. It's usually just one night a week, but it's like clockwork at this point. I mean, it's always when I'm alone, too. I'll get home from the sanctuary, and like I was saying, I'm just completely physically exhausted. I'll tell myself on the drive home, "Okay, you're just going to make a normal dinner, maybe some chicken and vegetables, something sensible," because my biology brain knows what my body actually needs after a long day of hauling feed and wrestling animals. But then I walk in the door, and the house is just so quiet. It's just me. And before I even realize what's happening, I'm opening the pantry, and then the fridge, and then it's like a switch flips in my brain. 

I'll start with something small, maybe a handful of crackers, but then it spirals so fast. I'll eat the whole box of crackers, and then a loaf of bread, and then maybe I'll order a massive pizza, or two, and I just eat and eat until I'm physically in pain. Far, far more than I ever meant to. And it's like I'm not even tasting it anymore, I'm just consuming it. And then, of course, the panic sets in. That suffocating feeling I mentioned earlier. And then I'm in the bathroom, making myself throw up, just trying to undo it all. 

It's exhausting, honestly. It's like this secret second job I have that I never applied for. And it's every single week. I keep thinking, "This week will be different, this week I'll break the cycle," but then Thursday or Friday night rolls around, and I'm exhausted, and I'm alone, and... well, it just happens again. It's been a solid four months of this routine, at least one night a week where the whole bingeing and throwing up thing just takes over my entire evening. It's incredibly frustrating because I know better, you know? I know the science of it, I know the physical toll it takes, but in that moment, all that logic just completely flies out the window.
Do you fear gaining weight when you binge eat?

Oh, God, yes. It's... honestly, it's terrifying. It's not just when I binge, either, it's this constant, looming dread that just hangs over me all the time. Like, I have this routine where I'll check my weight, usually right after a long shift at the sanctuary, when I'm already exhausted and covered in dirt and hay. And if I step on that scale and it's even a single pound higher—just one pound!—it completely derails me. 

Or, you know, with my work clothes. I wear these really thick, heavy-duty canvas work pants because, well, you need them when you're dealing with animal claws and scraping against wooden fences and concrete all day. They don't have any stretch to them at all. So if I pull them on in the morning before heading out, and they feel even slightly tighter around the waist, my brain just goes into absolute overdrive. 

I'll spend the entire day at work, while I'm supposed to be focusing on the animals, just completely agonizing over it. I'll be out there mucking a stall or feeding the pigs, and the whole time I'm just worrying that I'm letting myself get fat. It's this horrible, loud spiral in my head of "you're losing control, you're getting soft, you're letting yourself go." And then, almost automatically, I start planning how to make up for it. I'll be calculating in my head while I'm working, thinking, "Okay, I have to skip lunch today, I'll just drink black coffee, I'll take on the extra heavy lifting with the feed bags to burn more, I won't eat anything until tomorrow night." 

It just consumes my thoughts completely. Because in my head, gaining weight means I'm failing, you know? It means all that intense physical labor I do isn't enough, and it just... it drives me crazy. I just can't stand the thought of it. The panic of feeling my clothes not fit exactly the way they did yesterday is just so overwhelming, I can't focus on anything else until I figure out a plan to fix it.
How are you feeling emotionally right before one of these binge eating episodes starts?

Emotionally? Um... wow, I don't... I don't really know if I have a clear answer for that. Like, if you're asking if I'm sitting there feeling super sad, or angry, or, I don't know, crying about something? It's really not like that at all. I think people always assume there's this big emotional trigger, you know? Like on TV where someone has a horrible day or gets dumped and they just start eating everything in sight. But for me... I honestly haven't noticed feeling much of anything right before it starts. Emotionally, I mean. 

Physically, like I was saying before, I'm just completely drained from the sanctuary, my muscles are aching from the feed bags, I'm covered in dirt, but emotionally? It's almost like my brain is just... blank. It's like a void. I'm not stressed about the animals, I'm not upset about my life, I'm just... numb, I guess? But not numb in a depressed way, just... switched off. Like I'm on autopilot. I'll be walking through the front door, dropping my keys on the counter, taking off my boots, and I'm not thinking about my feelings at all. 

The emotional part—the absolute panic, the suffocating anxiety I was telling you about—that doesn't hit until *after* I've eaten, when the reality of what I've just done sets in. But leading up to it? Right before I take that first bite of whatever it is? I really couldn't tell you. There's no specific mood or feeling that I can pinpoint. It's just this strange absence of emotion, just a total blank slate until the switch flips and I'm already eating.
Is your fear of gaining weight the main reason you purge after binge eating?

Yeah. Yeah, exactly. It's... well, it's entirely about that. When I'm sitting there, right after the binge is over, and I'm just looking at the empty boxes or the wrappers, that's when the reality of it just completely crashes down on me. I start thinking about all the food I just consumed. Like, thousands of calories, just sitting there in my stomach like a lead weight. And my brain just goes into this absolute panic mode, picturing all of it turning into fat, making those heavy canvas work pants I told you about even tighter, basically undoing all the intense physical labor I did at the sanctuary all day. 

It's like a ticking clock in my head. I'll be sitting there, feeling so incredibly full, like physically in pain from how much I ate, and my brain is just screaming at me that I only have a very small window of time to fix this. So, after I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up because it feels like the only way to undo it before the calories settle in. 

I just have this terrifying image of my body absorbing all of it, and if I don't get it out right then and there, if I let it digest, then I've permanently ruined everything. And it's awful, it really is an awful thing to have to do, but in that moment, it's the only thing that gives me any relief from that absolute terror of gaining weight. It's like I'm hitting a reset button, or at least I try to convince myself I am. Because the alternative—just sitting there on the couch and letting my body process all that food—is just completely unthinkable to me. I would probably lose my mind just sitting there waiting for it to turn into weight. So, yeah, it's entirely about stopping those calories from settling in and changing my body.
Do you feel like you're losing control when you start eating during these episodes?

Yeah. Yeah, absolutely. It's... it's exactly like that. It's actually the main reason I finally decided to come in and talk to someone, because it's just getting so out of hand. Like I was saying, I get home from the sanctuary, and usually it's late, right? The sun is down, the house is completely quiet, I'm totally alone. And I'll just start eating. And it's not like I sit down and think, "I'm going to eat all of this." It starts with just one thing. But then... it's like a switch flips in my brain, or like something else completely takes over my body. 

It's the most bizarre, terrifying feeling. I'll be standing there in the kitchen, usually just in front of the open fridge or the pantry, not even bothering to put things on a plate half the time. And I'll be physically reaching for more food, shoving it in my mouth, and in my head, I'm screaming at myself. My inner monologue is literally going, "Stop, what are you doing? Put it away, close the door, just walk out of the kitchen, go to bed." I am fully aware that I shouldn't be doing it, and I'm actively telling myself to stop, but my hands just won't listen. 

It's like I'm a passenger in my own body. I'll just keep eating and eating, opening another box, unwrapping another thing, and I literally cannot force myself to stop until I'm so physically stuffed that it hurts, or until there's just nothing left that I want to eat. The disconnect between what my brain is telling me to do—which is to stop immediately—and what my body is actually doing is just... it's horrible. It makes me feel completely crazy. So, yeah, losing control doesn't even begin to cover it. It feels like I'm totally hijacked.
Do you ever try to burn off the calories from your binge eating episodes through excessive exercise?

Excessive exercise? No, not really. I mean, I guess it depends on how you define exercise, right? Because, like I was telling you, my whole day is essentially one long, grueling workout. Being an animal caretaker, especially at a large sanctuary, it's not like sitting at a desk. I'm up at dawn, and from the moment I get there, I'm moving. I'm hauling fifty-pound bags of feed across muddy fields, I'm mucking out stalls, I'm repairing fences, I'm wrangling animals that weigh ten times what I do. It's incredibly physical work, and by the time I get home, I'm just completely destroyed. My back aches, my knees hurt, my arms feel like they're made of lead. 

So the idea of coming home, having one of those... episodes, and then going for a run or hitting a gym? It's just physically impossible for me. I barely have the energy to drag myself up the stairs to my bedroom, let alone jump on a treadmill. And honestly, even on my days off, I'm usually so exhausted from the work week that I just want to lay flat on the floor and not move a single muscle. 

So, no, I don't try to exercise it off. That's why the throwing up thing is... well, it's the only option I feel like I have. Because I can't burn it off. There's just no gas left in the tank for that. If I had a desk job, maybe it would be different, maybe I'd be one of those people who runs ten miles after eating too much, but for me, the throwing up is the only way I can get rid of it without having to exert any more physical energy, because I just don't have any left to give.
Is your fear of gaining weight the primary reason you feel compelled to purge after binge eating?

Yeah, like I was saying earlier, it really is the whole driving force behind it. I know we kind of just touched on this, but I honestly cannot overstate how much that fear just completely consumes my thoughts. It's not just a passing worry, it's... well, to give you an idea of how bad it gets, if I step on the scale after a long shift at the sanctuary—and I weigh myself constantly, probably way more than I should—but if that number is even just a single pound higher than I think it should be, or, God forbid, if I'm getting dressed in the morning and those heavy canvas work pants feel even slightly tighter around my waist... my entire day is just completely derailed. 

I will literally spend the whole day out there, whether I'm feeding the animals or mucking out the barns, just agonizing over it. I'll be sweating, working my hands to the bone, and my mind is just racing, obsessing over the fact that I'm letting myself get fat. It's like this loud, blaring alarm going off in my head that I cannot mute, no matter how distracted I try to get with my work. And right away, the second I feel that tightness in my pants or see that number on the scale, I start planning exactly how I'm going to make up for it. 

My brain just starts calculating, you know? Figuring out how I can fix it, how I can get rid of anything I eat later, mapping out the whole evening just to ensure that one pound doesn't turn into two, or five, or ten. It's this constant, exhausting, never-ending loop. So when you ask if that fear is the primary reason I feel compelled to get rid of the food... yes, a hundred percent. Because living with that panic, that creeping, physical sensation that my clothes don't fit right and that my body is expanding... I just can't tolerate it. It dictates absolutely everything I do.
Do you ever fast or restrict your food intake after one of these binge eating episodes?

Fasting? Um... no. No, I really don't do that. And it's not because I don't want to, believe me. The morning after one of those nights, the absolute last thing I want to do is put anything else in my stomach. The guilt is just... it's suffocating, and the idea of eating again makes my skin crawl. But practically speaking? I just can't. 

It really goes back to what I was saying earlier about the sanctuary and how incredibly physical the job is. If I try to go to work on an empty stomach, especially after... you know, after throwing up the night before... I would literally pass out in the middle of a paddock. I mean, just the other week, we had this massive delivery of alfalfa bales, and I was out there in the heat, stacking them in the barn for three hours straight. If I hadn't eaten breakfast, I wouldn't have made it through the first twenty minutes. 

Or, you know, if I'm trying to corral one of the rescue horses—we have this one, a draft cross, huge guy, easily eighteen hundred pounds, and he can get pretty spooky with loud noises. You have to be completely alert, totally grounded, and physically ready to hold your own if he pulls back on the lead rope. You cannot be lightheaded or have your hands shaking because you decided to skip meals to make up for a binge. It's actually a safety hazard for me and for the animals if I'm not physically operating at a hundred percent. 

So, no matter how much I hate myself the next morning, no matter how much my brain is screaming at me to just zip my mouth shut and not eat a single calorie for the next twenty-four hours, I force myself to eat. I'll have breakfast, usually oatmeal or eggs, something that will stick to my ribs and actually give me the energy to do my job. And then I'll eat lunch, too, usually with the rest of the crew in the breakroom, so I look completely normal to everyone else. 

It's such a weird disconnect, honestly. Because during the day, I'm eating like a totally regular, healthy guy who just needs fuel for heavy manual labor. I don't restrict my food at all during the shift. I eat exactly what I need to survive the day and get the work done. It's only when the sun goes down and I'm back in that empty, quiet house that everything just... unravels again. So, yeah, no fasting. I just rely on the other thing to fix it.
Is the fear of gaining weight what drives you to purge after binge eating?

Yeah, I know we just talked about the weight thing, but it's like... it's all connected, you know? It's like this chain reaction. The fear of getting fat, like I was saying, is always there, always humming in the background while I'm at the sanctuary, while I'm stacking hay or whatever. And then the binge happens, and it's like that fear just explodes into this full-blown panic. It's so intense, it's almost hard to breathe. 

So, yeah, that fear is exactly why I do what I do afterwards. Because after I eat like that—after I've just consumed thousands of calories in sitting on my kitchen floor, surrounded by wrappers and empty boxes, feeling like my stomach is stretched so tight it might actually tear—I can't just sit there with it. I can't just let it sit in my stomach and process. The panic is screaming at me that if I don't get it out right that second, every single ounce of that food is going to instantly turn into fat, and I'll wake up the next morning and my work pants won't button, and I'll be exactly what I'm terrified of becoming. 

So, I usually end up right in the bathroom, hunched over the toilet, making myself throw up. It's awful, it really is. It hurts my throat, it makes my eyes water, it leaves me feeling shaky and disgusting, but in that moment, it feels like the absolute only way to undo what I just did. It feels like this desperate race against the clock to get it all out before the calories have a chance to settle in and do their damage. If I don't do it, the anxiety is just... it's unbearable. I wouldn't be able to sleep, I wouldn't be able to function the next day at work. So, yeah, the fear of the weight gain is exactly what pushes me into that bathroom every single time. It's the only way I can hit the reset button, or at least, that's what it feels like.
Do you ever use any methods other than throwing up to try to compensate for the calories you consumed during a binge eating episode?

Other methods? Um... no. No, not really. I know I literally just said this, like, two seconds ago, so I'm sorry for repeating myself, but it really is just the throwing up. I don't mess around with, like, pills or whatever else people might use, and I definitely don't try to go to the gym and run on a treadmill for hours because, like I explained with the sanctuary, my entire day is already one giant, exhausting workout. By the time I get home from hauling hay and wrangling thousand-pound animals, my muscles are aching, my back is sore, and I'm completely wiped out. I barely have the energy to stand, let alone do extra cardio. 

So, no, I don't exercise it off, and I don't fast, as we talked about. It really just comes down to exactly what I was just explaining to you. After I eat like that, after all those wrappers are empty and that heavy, sickening fullness hits my stomach... I usually end up right back in the bathroom, making myself throw up, because it really feels like the absolute only way to undo it before the calories settle in. 

If I were to try anything else, it just wouldn't be fast enough, you know? Like, the food would still be *inside* me, digesting, turning into weight while I waited for some other method to work. And my brain just cannot handle that thought. The panic is so immediate, so visceral, that I need an immediate fix. I need it gone right that second. So, yeah, it's always the bathroom. Just me, sitting on the cold tiles, leaning over the toilet. It's an incredibly grim routine, and I hate how much it controls me, but in my head, it's the only option that actually works fast enough to stop the damage. So, no, nothing else. Just that.
Have you been having these episodes of binge eating followed by purging at least twice a week for the past three months?

Twice a week? Um... no, not quite twice a week. And actually, it's been going on a bit longer than three months. If I really stop and think about it, looking back at the calendar and what we were doing at work... it really started getting into this specific pattern right around the time we had this massive intake of neglected alpacas at the sanctuary, which was just this huge, exhausting logistical nightmare. That was at least four months ago. So, yeah, for at least the last four months, this has been happening. 

But as for how often, it's usually just once a week. There has usually been at least one night each week where it all just completely falls apart. You know, I'll push through the first few days of the week, working myself to the bone, keeping everything totally together, eating my normal meals with the crew like I told you. But then, inevitably, there's that one night where the physical exhaustion and the mental stress just peak, and I'm completely alone in my house. The sanctuary is quiet, my phone finally stops ringing, the sun is down, and I just... I end up eating far, far more than I ever meant to. I'll start with what I think is just going to be a regular dinner, telling myself I'm just refueling my body after a hard day, but then I just can't stop. 

And then, exactly like I was just explaining with the panic and the fear of the weight gain... I make myself throw up afterward. It's like this weekly ritual that I absolutely despise. I spend the whole week dreading it, knowing that one of these nights, usually when my muscles are just screaming and the house feels way too empty, I'm going to lose control again. I always tell myself, 'This week will be different, this week I'll just eat a normal dinner, read a book, and go straight to sleep,' but then that one night hits, and the cycle just repeats itself all over again. So, yeah, not twice a week, but pretty much one night every single week for the last four months. It's just so frustrating that I can't seem to break that one night's hold on me.
Do you always make yourself throw up after these binge eating episodes?

Yeah, I... I know we're kind of circling back to this, and I feel like a bit of a broken record here since we just touched on it, but yes. Every single time. Like I was saying before, there's never been a time where I have one of those nights—where I just completely lose control and eat all that food—and then just go to bed. I literally can't. My brain just won't allow it. 

So, yeah, after I eat like that, when all the food is gone and I'm just sitting there in the aftermath, feeling so incredibly full and heavy and just... disgusted with myself... I always end up right back in the bathroom. It's just the automatic next step in the routine. I make myself throw up because, exactly like I was trying to explain earlier, it really feels like the absolute only way to undo it before the calories have a chance to settle in and become permanent. 

If I don't do it, the panic just takes over entirely. I'll just sit there on the floor imagining every single bite turning into weight on my body, ruining all the hard physical work I do at the sanctuary. So it's not even really a choice anymore, you know? It's just... I eat, the panic hits, and I go straight to the toilet to get rid of it. Every single time. I wish I could say there were nights where I just rode out the anxiety and let my body digest it, but... no. It always ends the exact same way.
Have you been having these episodes of binge eating followed by purging at least once a week for the past three months?

Yeah, I know I'm probably repeating myself again, and I'm sorry for talking in circles, but yes, that's exactly it. Like I was saying a few minutes ago, it's been going on for at least four months now. It really started ramping up during that massive alpaca rescue we did, which was just this incredibly stressful, chaotic time at the sanctuary. And since then, for those four months, it's been pretty consistently happening once a week. 

I'll get through most of the week just fine, working hard, eating normally with the crew, but then there's always that one night. If I hadn't eaten breakfast, I wouldn't have made it through the first twenty minutes. 

Or, you know, if I'm trying to corral one of the rescue horses—we have this one, a draft cross, huge guy, easily eighteen hundred pounds, and he can get pretty spooky with loud noises. You have to be completely alert, totally grounded, and physically ready to hold your own if he pulls back on the lead rope. You cannot be lightheaded or have your hands shaking because you decided to skip meals to make up for a binge. It's actually a safety hazard for me and for the animals if I'm not physically operating at a hundred percent. 

So, no matter how much I hate myself the next morning, no matter how much my brain is screaming at me to just zip my mouth shut and not eat a single calorie for the next twenty-four hours, I force myself to eat. I'll have breakfast, usually oatmeal or eggs, something that will stick to my ribs and actually give me the energy to do my job. And then I'll eat lunch, too, usually with the rest of the crew in the breakroom, so I look completely normal to everyone else. 

It's such a weird disconnect, honestly. Because during the day, I'm eating like a totally regular, healthy guy who just needs fuel for heavy manual labor. I don't restrict my food at all during the shift. I eat exactly what I need to survive the day and get the work done. It's only when the sun goes down and I'm back in that empty, quiet house that everything just... unravels again. So, yeah, no fasting. I just rely on the other thing to fix it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's binge eating episodes are accompanied by a fear of gaining weight that is characteristic of bulimia nervosa
doctor.question: Is the fear of gaining weight what drives you to purge after binge eating?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
target_item.manifestation: After I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up because it feels like the only way to undo it before the calories settle in.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the motivation behind the purging behavior (preventing weight gain), which directly corresponds to the compensatory behavior of purging to undo the caloric intake.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I know we just talked about the weight thing, but it's like... it's all connected, you know? It's like this chain reaction. The fear of getting fat, like I was saying, is always there, always humming in the background while I'm at the sanctuary, while I'm stacking hay or whatever. And then the binge happens, and it's like that fear just explodes into this full-blown panic. It's so intense, it's almost hard to breathe. 

So, yeah, that fear is exactly why I do what I do afterwards. Because after I eat like that—after I've just consumed thousands of calories in sitting on my kitchen floor, surrounded by wrappers and empty boxes, feeling like my stomach is stretched so tight it might actually tear—I can't just sit there with it. I can't just let it sit in my stomach and process. The panic is screaming at me that if I don't get it out right that second, every single ounce of that food is going to instantly turn into fat, and I'll wake up the next morning and my work pants won't button, and I'll be exactly what I'm terrified of becoming. 

So, I usually end up right in the bathroom, hunched over the toilet, making myself throw up. It's awful, it really is. It hurts my throat, it makes my eyes water, it leaves me feeling shaky and disgusting, but in that moment, it feels like the absolute only way to undo what I just did. It feels like this desperate race against the clock to get it all out before the calories have a chance to settle in and do their damage. If I don't do it, the anxiety is just... it's unbearable. I wouldn't be able to sleep, I wouldn't be able to function the next day at work. So, yeah, the fear of the weight gain is exactly what pushes me into that bathroom every single time. It's the only way I can hit the reset button, or at least, that's what it feels like.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's binge eating episodes are followed by compensatory behaviors other than purging
doctor.question: Do you ever use any methods other than throwing up to try to compensate for the calories you consumed during a binge eating episode?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
target_item.manifestation: After I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up because it feels like the only way to undo it before the calories settle in.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about other methods of compensatory behaviors (besides vomiting) used to prevent weight gain, which falls under the category of inappropriate compensatory behaviors.

patient.answer:
Other methods? Um... no. No, not really. I know I literally just said this, like, two seconds ago, so I'm sorry for repeating myself, but it really is just the throwing up. I don't mess around with, like, pills or whatever else people might use, and I definitely don't try to go to the gym and run on a treadmill for hours because, like I explained with the sanctuary, my entire day is already one giant, exhausting workout. By the time I get home from hauling hay and wrangling thousand-pound animals, my muscles are aching, my back is sore, and I'm completely wiped out. I barely have the energy to stand, let alone do extra cardio. 

So, no, I don't exercise it off, and I don't fast, as we talked about. It really just comes down to exactly what I was just explaining to you. After I eat like that, after all those wrappers are empty and that heavy, sickening fullness hits my stomach... I usually end up right back in the bathroom, making myself throw up, because it really feels like the absolute only way to undo it before the calories settle in. 

If I were to try anything else, it just wouldn't be fast enough, you know? Like, the food would still be *inside* me, digesting, turning into weight while I waited for some other method to work. And my brain just cannot handle that thought. The panic is so immediate, so visceral, that I need an immediate fix. I need it gone right that second. So, yeah, it's always the bathroom. Just me, sitting on the cold tiles, leaning over the toilet. It's an incredibly grim routine, and I hate how much it controls me, but in my head, it's the only option that actually works fast enough to stop the damage. So, no, nothing else. Just that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior meets the frequency criteria for Bulimia Nervosa
doctor.question: Have you been having these episodes of binge eating followed by purging at least twice a week for the past three months?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: For at least the last four months, there has usually been at least one night each week where I eat far more than I meant to when I'm alone, and then I make myself throw up afterward.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the frequency and duration of the binge eating and purging episodes, which directly corresponds to the criteria for how often these behaviors must occur.

patient.answer:
Twice a week? Um... no, not quite twice a week. And actually, it's been going on a bit longer than three months. If I really stop and think about it, looking back at the calendar and what we were doing at work... it really started getting into this specific pattern right around the time we had this massive intake of neglected alpacas at the sanctuary, which was just this huge, exhausting logistical nightmare. That was at least four months ago. So, yeah, for at least the last four months, this has been happening. 

But as for how often, it's usually just once a week. There has usually been at least one night each week where it all just completely falls apart. You know, I'll push through the first few days of the week, working myself to the bone, keeping everything totally together, eating my normal meals with the crew like I told you. But then, inevitably, there's that one night where the physical exhaustion and the mental stress just peak, and I'm completely alone in my house. The sanctuary is quiet, my phone finally stops ringing, the sun is down, and I just... I end up eating far, far more than I ever meant to. I'll start with what I think is just going to be a regular dinner, telling myself I'm just refueling my body after a hard day, but then I just can't stop. 

And then, exactly like I was just explaining with the panic and the fear of the weight gain... I make myself throw up afterward. It's like this weekly ritual that I absolutely despise. I spend the whole week dreading it, knowing that one of these nights, usually when my muscles are just screaming and the house feels way too empty, I'm going to lose control again. I always tell myself, 'This week will be different, this week I'll just eat a normal dinner, read a book, and go straight to sleep,' but then that one night hits, and the cycle just repeats itself all over again. So, yeah, not twice a week, but pretty much one night every single week for the last four months. It's just so frustrating that I can't seem to break that one night's hold on me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's binge eating episodes are followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors, such as self-induced vomiting, to clarify the diagnosis between Bulimia Nervosa (F50.2) and Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.8)

patient.answer:
Yeah, I... I know we're kind of circling back to this, and I feel like a bit of a broken record here since we just touched on it, but yes. Every single time. Like I was saying before, there's never been a time where I have one of those nights—where I just completely lose control and eat all that food—and then just go to bed. I literally can't. My brain just won't allow it. 

So, yeah, after I eat like that, when all the food is gone and I'm just sitting there in the aftermath, feeling so incredibly full and heavy and just... disgusted with myself... I always end up right back in the bathroom. It's just the automatic next step in the routine. I make myself throw up because, exactly like I was trying to explain earlier, it really feels like the absolute only way to undo it before the calories have a chance to settle in and become permanent. 

If I don't do it, the panic just takes over entirely. I'll just sit there on the floor imagining every single bite turning into weight on my body, ruining all the hard physical work I do at the sanctuary. So it's not even really a choice anymore, you know? It's just... I eat, the panic hits, and I go straight to the toilet to get rid of it. Every single time. I wish I could say there were nights where I just rode out the anxiety and let my body digest it, but... no. It always ends the exact same way.
